justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current market price around $430 for the underlying asset (likely SPY or a similar broad equity index). At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a small positive bias, reflecting the historically slight positive drift in equity markets on any given day. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to $434, consistent with an annualized drift assumption applied over five trading days. At the one-month horizon, the $438 estimate reflects that same drift extrapolated further, though the incremental gain is modest because drift alone is a weak signal relative to the noise that accumulates over longer periods.

The confidence interval widths were driven primarily by realized and implied volatility assumptions. At the one-day horizon, typical daily volatility for a large-cap equity index is roughly 0.5–1%, which produces a relatively tight band of about plus or minus $16. Over one week, volatility scales by the square root of time, widening the interval to roughly plus or minus $29. Over one month, this scaling continues, yielding an interval of approximately plus or minus $58. I also factored in that options markets and recent realized volatility can diverge from long-run averages, so I tried to reflect a slightly elevated uncertainty environment rather than assuming perfectly calm conditions.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a sharper-than-expected rise in unemployment, a credit event, or an escalation in geopolitical tensions — could trigger a sharp sell-off exceeding the lower bounds of my confidence intervals. A surprise hawkish pivot from a major central bank, particularly the Federal Reserve signaling additional rate hikes, could also compress valuations rapidly. On the upside, a blowout earnings season, a surprisingly benign inflation print, or a significant de-escalation in an ongoing geopolitical conflict could drive prices above my upper bounds.

It is also worth acknowledging structural uncertainty in my estimates themselves. I do not have real-time market data, so my anchor price and volatility assumptions may already be stale. If the true current price differs meaningfully from my assumed starting point, all three estimates shift accordingly. Additionally, tail risks — such as a flash crash, a major financial institution failing, or an unexpected policy shock — are inherently underweighted in interval estimates derived from normal-distribution assumptions, meaning genuine black swan events could place outcomes well outside even my stated 90% confidence intervals.
